newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha's party predicts Albania election win.
newsitem.headline: Berisha's party predicts Albania election win.

text.p: A senior official in Albanian President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party forecast an easy win in Sunday's general election and said the party would form an alliance with other groups to restore order.

The opposition Socialists, who have also predicted victory, denounced Berisha's increasingly aggressive campaign and said he was bent on stirring rather than quelling violence in the former communist country.

Genc Pollo, the Democratic Party's Secretary General, said the president was committed to forming "the broadest possible coalition" after the election, which is seen by many as passing judgment on Berisha's five years in power.
"We believe the Democratic Party and its allies are bound to have a victory with almost 50 percent of the general vote and an absolute majority of the seats," Pollo told a news conference in English.
"We remain committed to the result of free and fair elections if that's the case and intend to cooperate with any political force after the election."
But that did not mean a coalition between the Democratic Party and the Socialists. He believed Berisha was "not prepared for 'cohabitation' if the Democratic Party was in opposition.
Although Berisha's job is not on the line in the vote, he has been waging a high-profile campaign to defend the huge majority the Democrats won in June 1996 election.
Observers inside and outside Albania say that vote was unfair. There have been no reliable polls for Sunday's vote.

Berisha has adopted an increasingly shrill tone in accusing the Socialists of fomenting the armed violence which has riven Albania since hundreds of thousands of people lost their life savings in shady investment schemes.
About 1,500 people have died.

The official news agency ATA said Berisha told a rally in the southeastern town of Maliq that he would establish law and order throughout Albania "within 75 days, and within 100 days all the effects of the communist rebellion will be overcome".

On Monday, he told Tirana supporters that the Socialists would "not enjoy the fruits of victory if they resort to terror or bloodshed" and meet the same demise as the hardline communists who ran the country for 45 years.
His Democrats would "wipe the smiles off their faces".
The Socialists, who are the heirs to Albania's Stalinist old guard but say they now support market values, said the statement proved Berisha would not abide by any vote going against him.
"Berisha keeps a dagger between his teeth and surrounds himself with armed hordes to stain Albania with blood, to destabilise it completely," a party statement said.
Albania's main political parties signed an agreement in Rome on Monday pledging to cooperate for a free, fair vote.
Socialist leader Fatos Nano promised to honour any result but said he had "no possibility" of losing.
He contended that gangs "acting under Berisha's orders" could destroy ballot papers.
Berisha was forced to call the early election at the height of the March violence and agree to the appointment of an interim government led by the Socialists.
A 7,000-strong multinational force has maintained a degree of order in the mountainous Balkan country, Europe's poorest, and more than 450 international monitors will oversee the vote.
But mafia-style gangs still control many districts, particularly in the south. Several dozen people have died in the past week alone.

The chairman of the Central Election Commission said Berisha had turned down a request to close polling stations by 7 p.m., two hours earlier than planned, in order to bring all ballots in by nightfall.
Officials quoted Berisha as saying there was no legal mechanism to make the change, which was backed by all parties.
